title: Gratitude
hookLine: the grateful heart sees gifts everywhere
tomorrow: can you feast on the same day you cried?

cards: The package lands on the porch, the app asks you to rate the driver, and the app is closed before the stars load. Now a road between Samaria and Galilee.
Ten men with leprosy stand far off and shout across it: Jesus, Master, have mercy on us. He calls back: go, show yourselves to the priests. On the way, all ten are healed.
Nine keep walking. One turns around, praising God out loud, and falls at Jesus' feet. And Jesus asks, “Were there not ten cleansed? but where are the nine?”

teach.b: The nine weren't wicked. They did exactly what they'd been told. They got the gift and kept going.

In this story, gratitude is the turn: seeing where the healing came from, and going back. Paul pushes it further: “In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you.” Read it closely.

teach.h: IN EVERY THING, NOT FOR EVERY THING.
teach.b: In every thing, not for every thing. Paul isn't asking anyone to be thankful for a loss or a diagnosis. He's saying there is something to thank God for inside every situation, even a hard one.

teach.h: EVERY GOOD GIFT IS FROM ABOVE.
teach.b: James names the source: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights.” And Paul asks a blunt question: “what hast thou that thou didst not receive?” Breath.
A body. A language someone taught you. Start counting, and the list keeps going.
Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight: the one who turned back was a Samaritan, and Jesus calls him “this stranger.”
The outsider is the one who noticed. Christians describe gratitude less as a mood that visits and more as a way of seeing, practiced until it sticks.
Some say grace before meals for that reason: a small turn back before eating.

how: Christians give thanks in many forms: some say grace before meals, some name blessings in prayer at night, and churches build thanksgiving into their worship; the story of the ten lepers is a common picture of turning back to thank God.

o: seeing what you have as given, and saying thanks
feeling you owe someone a debt to repay soon
saying thank you politely so you seem kind

games.q: who did what on the road — tap the pairs.

s: the nine who kept walking disobeyed Jesus
they did exactly what he told them: go, show yourselves to the priests. they just never turned back.
all ten healed men came back to thank Jesus
only one returned, and Jesus asked, where are the nine?
the man who came back was a Samaritan
Luke adds that detail, and Jesus calls him “this stranger.”

games.q: a café regular finally gets the table by the window she's asked about for weeks. the next morning she comes in just to say thanks. what did she do that the nine didn't?
o: she turned back to name where the gift came from.
she followed the café's rules exactly.
she felt grateful inside, which is all that counts.
games.why: in Luke, all ten were healed and all ten obeyed. gratitude was the turn: one went back.

practice: Ten were healed, so count ten gifts, slowly, one at a time, on your fingers: a person, a meal, a word someone said, this breath. When you reach ten, rest with the list.
If you pray, turn back like the one who came and say thank you.

wordCard.voice: Gratitude. Seeing what you have as given, and turning back to say thank you for it.

orig.note: Greek 'to give thanks,' the verb behind 'give thanks' in Paul's line.

carryVoice: Your line: everything is gift. Even the breath you just counted, one of ten. Day seventeen thirty-seven.
